case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s bar on relitigating previously presented claims in “second or successive” habeas applications, 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1), applies to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions to vacate sentence under 28 U.S.C. §2255—and, if so, whether Supreme Court review is jurisdictionally blocked by §2244(b)(3)(E).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 2244(b)(1), 2244(b)(3)(E), and 2255 (including AEDPA’s second-or-successive framework and related timing provisions such as §2255(f)(3)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1) by its text governs only state-prisoner habeas petitions under §2254 (“application under section 2254”), not federal prisoners’ §2255 motions, so the Eleventh Circuit’s rule (treating §2244(b)(1) as applicable to §2255 via §2255(h)’s cross-reference to §2244) wrongly forecloses meritorious claims—especially claims relying on new, retroactive Supreme Court decisions—before a federal court can consider them; he further contends the Court should not treat §2244(b)(3)(E) as eliminating Supreme Court certiorari jurisdiction to resolve the acknowledged circuit split, because otherwise an entrenched conflict on an important federal question becomes effectively unreviewable.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States maintains that applying §2244(b)(1) to §2255 is consistent with AEDPA’s structure and finality goals: Congress intentionally tightened second-or-successive review, and federal prisoners are not unfairly disadvantaged because they already had prior opportunities to raise claims (direct appeal plus an initial §2255), and AEDPA expressly tolerates 'harsh results' (as reflected in the limitations rule of §2255(f)(3) and Dodd) that prevent diligent prisoners from benefiting from later legal developments; on jurisdiction, the government position (as reflected in the record’s discussion of §2244(b)(3)(E)) is that the statute’s “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari” language restricts Supreme Court review of courts of appeals’ authorization decisions for second-or-successive filings, limiting the Court’s ability to reach the merits in the ordinary certiorari posture.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., statement respecting denial of certiorari)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (Sotomayor, J., statement respecting denial)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the strongest textual objection: §2244(b)(1) speaks only to an “application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) does not expressly mention (b)(1). But §2255(h) makes a successive §2255 motion available only if it is “certified as provided in section 2244,” and as Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize, §2244(b)’s certification regime is an integrated set of mandatory threshold gates that begins with (b)(1)’s relitigation bar; otherwise the cross-reference invites repetitive federal-prisoner claims that AEDPA’s finality- and delay-reduction design was meant to foreclose. On jurisdiction, I remain persuaded by Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar on certiorari review of authorization decisions “under this subsection” cannot be evaded by relabeling the dispute as an “antecedent legal error,” which would effectively rewrite Congress’s rigid limit. Given AEDPA’s structure and our consistent insistence on enforcing its threshold constraints as written, I would affirm.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the strongest textual point: §2244(b)(1) speaks of a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) does not name (b)(1). But §2255(h) conditions the very availability of a successive §2255 motion on being “certified as provided in section 2244,” and—consistent with the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s structural account—that cross-reference is most naturally read to incorporate §2244(b)’s integrated gatekeeping scheme, whose first mandatory filter is (b)(1)’s relitigation bar; otherwise AEDPA’s successive-motion limits become partly futile for federal prisoners. Justice Sotomayor’s “antecedent legal error” theory does not overcome §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical command that our Court may not review an authorization determination “under this subsection,” because carving out review whenever a petitioner alleges misapplied prerequisites would rewrite a rule-like jurisdictional bar into an exception. Nor does constitutional avoidance justify that revision absent a serious Suspension Clause problem, and the loss of an extra collateral pathway beyond direct review and an initial §2255 motion is not such a problem.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the best textual point: §2244(b)(1) speaks of a “habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) does not name (b)(1). But §2255(h) conditions the very availability of a second-or-successive §2255 motion on being “certified as provided in section 2244,” and—as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett explain—that cross-reference sensibly imports the integrated gatekeeping scheme, including the threshold relitigation bar, or else Congress’s design invites repetitive recycling of old claims in a new filing posture. On jurisdiction, I remain aligned with Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar forecloses our review of an authorization determination “under this subsection,” and Justice Sotomayor’s “antecedent legal error” theory risks creating an atextual exception that would swallow the rule. The structural and system-design consequences AEDPA was enacted to address—finality, delay reduction, and conserving federal judicial resources—support adhering to the statute’s screening architecture as a whole rather than carving out (b)(1) based on a phrase that can be understood as describing the origin of the gatekeeping model rather than limiting what §2255(h) incorporates.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Alito’s strongest structural point that §2255(h)’s phrase “certified as provided in section 2244” sounds like Congress borrowed an integrated gatekeeping regime. But the integrated-regime reading cannot overcome the enacted limitation in §2244(b)(1) to a “habeas corpus application under section 2254” without treating that phrase as surplusage, and AEDPA’s cross-references elsewhere show Congress knew how to extend particular restrictions across the §2254/§2255 divide when it wished. As Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the better reading is that §2255(h) incorporates §2244(b)(2)–(3)’s certification standards and procedure, not a §2254-only relitigation bar Congress did not extend. On jurisdiction, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Gorsuch’s and the Chief’s broad reading of §2244(b)(3)(E): it should bar review of the authorization disposition itself, not foreclose correcting a court of appeals’ antecedent error about which statutory gatekeeping rules apply at all.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Alito make the best structural case that §2244(b) is an integrated gatekeeping scheme and that §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” might be read to import that package wholesale. But that argument cannot overcome the enacted trigger Congress chose: §2244(b)(1) by its terms governs only a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and treating §2255(h)’s cross-reference as silently erasing that limitation is not “structural coherence,” it is amendment by implication. And on jurisdiction, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E): a certiorari bar on “authoriz[ation] under this subsection” cannot sensibly insulate a threshold mistake about whether the court of appeals applied a subsection that does not apply to §2255 at all. The better reading—consistent with our term-of-art approach to successive filings—is that §2255(h) incorporates §2244(b)(2)–(3)’s certification standards and procedures, not §2244(b)(1)’s §2254-only relitigation command.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan put their finger on the hardest textual point—§2244(b)(1) speaks of an "application under section 2254"—and I do not dismiss that limiting phrase. But §2255(h) makes successive §2255 authority turn on certification "as provided in section 2244," and as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, §2244(b) is not a menu of detachable items but an integrated set of mandatory threshold conditions whose screening begins with the relitigation rule; reading the cross-reference to omit (b)(1) invites a structural loophole at odds with AEDPA’s finality-focused design. Separately, even if incorporation were debatable, §2244(b)(3)(E) bars our review of an authorization determination "under this subsection," and Justice Sotomayor’s proposed "antecedent error" carveout would convert a categorical jurisdictional limit into an atextual exception. Under AEDPA’s cumulative scheme, Bowe fails at the statutory gate, so we need not proceed to any merits or equitable inquiries.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is structural: §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” sounds like an integrated gatekeeping package that would naturally include §2244(b)(1). But structural coherence cannot override enacted text, and §2244(b)(1) expressly applies only to a “habeas corpus application under section 2254”; reading §2255(h)’s cross-reference to silently erase that limitation stretches “as provided” beyond the certification procedure/criteria and effectively amends (b)(1)’s trigger. On jurisdiction, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Thomas’s view that §2244(b)(3)(E) bars review here, because the antecedent question is whether the court of appeals applied a statutory restriction that does not apply to §2255 at all—otherwise a persistent circuit split on governing law becomes insulated from correction. The Government’s concession that prior circuit precedent was inconsistent with the statute’s words further reinforces that the better course is to enforce the text as written and reverse.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the best textual objection—§2244(b)(1) is written for §2254 applications—but §2255(h) makes the filing of a successive §2255 motion depend on being “certified as provided in section 2244,” and that certification regime operates as an integrated set of threshold screens, as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito explain. Reading the cross-reference to import (b)(2)–(3) while excluding (b)(1) is not a neutral act of “respecting surplusage”; it creates a loophole Congress had strong reason to close in AEDPA’s funneling design, permitting repetitive federal-prisoner relitigation that state prisoners cannot pursue. On jurisdiction, I remain persuaded by Justice Gorsuch (and the Chief) that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s bar on certiorari review of an authorization determination “under this subsection” is categorical; recasting the question as an “antecedent legal error” risks an advisory pronouncement untethered to a reviewable merits judgment and would effectively rewrite Congress’s jurisdictional limit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s structural concern seriously: §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244” sounds like Congress wanted a unified gatekeeping scheme and a relitigation bar does important work in that architecture. But the enacted text regulates specific statutory objects, and §2244(b)(1) by its terms applies only to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254”; importing it into §2255 via a general cross-reference would effectively amend the trigger Congress wrote, contrary to our term-of-art approach in Banister/Magwood and our insistence (Gonzalez) on parsing “claims” and “applications” as Congress defined them. The “loophole” argument cannot justify treating §2254-only language as surplusage when §2255(h) already imposes strict hurdles (new evidence/new rule) and pre-AEDPA practice allowed limited successive review as a miscarriage-of-justice safety valve. On jurisdiction, I remain aligned with Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan: reading §2244(b)(3)(E) to insulate a court of appeals’ antecedent legal error about what gatekeeping rules apply at all would make unauthorized expansions of AEDPA effectively unreviewable.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA’s structure reflects a deliberate effort to curb serial collateral attacks and promote finality, and §2255(h)’s direction that a federal prisoner may file a second-or-successive motion only if it is “certified as provided in section 2244” is best read to incorporate the full gatekeeping package Congress created for repeat filings, including §2244(b)(1)’s bar on relitigating claims already presented. That reading respects Congress’s choice to impose strict threshold limits on federal-court authority rather than invite case-by-case equitable exceptions whenever later precedent appears favorable. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s targeted text bars certiorari review of the court of appeals’ authorization determination; nothing in this posture supplies an independent, nonbarred merits judgment to review, so the statute forecloses ordinary Supreme Court review even if that leaves a split unresolved. The petitioner’s fairness arguments, while substantial, cannot overcome AEDPA’s text-and-structure-based limits as this Court emphasized in applying similarly rigid timing and successive-filing rules.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Reading AEDPA as an integrated scheme, §2255(h)’s direction that a federal prisoner may file a second-or-successive motion only if it is “certified as provided in section 2244” is best understood to incorporate §2244’s successive-application constraints—including §2244(b)(1)’s bar on re-presenting claims—so that prisoners cannot use §2255 to accomplish what AEDPA forbids elsewhere. Accepting petitioner’s narrower, §2254-only reading would create a structural loophole for federal prisoners that would dilute AEDPA’s “carefully crafted limits” and risk rendering the successive-motion regime (including gatekeeping) partly futile. And where the court of appeals’ order is an authorization (or denial of authorization) decision under §2244(b)(3), §2244(b)(3)(E) speaks in jurisdictional, rule-like terms (“shall not … be the subject of … a writ of certiorari”), so this Court cannot reach the merits through ordinary certiorari review. Constitutional-avoidance does not alter that result absent a truly serious Suspension Clause problem; the loss of an additional collateral pathway beyond the initial §2255 and direct review is not enough to trigger that canon.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA establishes a distinct, statute-driven screening regime for “second or successive” collateral attacks, and §2255(h)’s cross-reference to §2244(b) is best read to incorporate the full claim-categorization structure that Congress adopted—mandatory dismissal of previously presented claims under §2244(b)(1) and tightly cabined review of truly new claims under §2244(b)(2). Accepting petitioner’s reading would create a sizable loophole for repetitive federal-prisoner litigation, frustrating AEDPA’s central design goals of finality and docket control by allowing relitigation of claims already aired in an initial §2255. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s plain command that the authorization decision “shall not be … the subject of … a writ of certiorari” forecloses this Court’s review in the ordinary certiorari posture of the court of appeals’ gatekeeping determination, and Congress is entitled to allocate review in this specialized habeas regime. The asserted equity concerns about later retroactive decisions cannot override the statutory structure, especially given AEDPA’s acceptance of “harsh results” in timing and successive-petition rules.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Reading AEDPA’s “second or successive” limits as terms of art informed by habeas history and statutory text, §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar applies by its own terms only to an “application under section 2254,” and §2255(h)’s limited cross-reference to §2244 imports the gatekeeping mechanism and criteria, not an additional, textually state-prisoner-specific relitigation rule. Treating §2244(b)(1) as silently governing §2255 would let a court of appeals expand AEDPA’s restrictions beyond what Congress wrote, upsetting AEDPA’s careful structure and collapsing the distinct §2254/§2255 schemes. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) is best read narrowly to preclude this Court’s review of individualized authorization determinations, not to insulate a court of appeals’ threshold legal error about what statutory requirements apply in the first place—otherwise, legally irrelevant barriers could become unreviewable. Applied here, the Eleventh Circuit’s denial of authorization rested on a requirement (§2244(b)(1)) inapplicable to §2255, so certiorari is not jurisdictionally barred and petitioner is entitled to have his request evaluated under the proper §2255(h) standards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with the text and the scheme Congress enacted: §2244(b)(1) expressly bars relitigation only for an "application under section 2254," and §2255(h) imports (by cross-reference) only the gatekeeping certification standards of §2244(b)(2) and (b)(3)—not §2244(b)(1)’s separate, §2254-specific relitigation bar. Treating “second or successive” and “application” as habeas terms of art (Gonzalez; Slack; Panetti), a §2255 motion is not automatically assimilated to a §2254 “application” for every §2244(b) consequence, especially where Congress wrote a selective cross-reference; the better reading is that the imported rules go no further than the provisions §2255(h) actually invokes. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s “certiorari” bar is triggered only as to an order “under this subsection” about a habeas “application,” and absent a clear statement that Congress meant to foreclose this Court’s review for federal prisoners’ §2255 litigation over what §2255(h) incorporates, I would not read the statute to close the Court’s doors to resolving an acknowledged circuit conflict. That approach keeps the postconviction scheme coherent and preserves §2255’s role as a remedy commensurate with habeas without silently adding extra restrictions Congress did not enact.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: AEDPA supplies mandatory, cumulative threshold conditions, and we must apply them as written when Congress has provided a valid rule of decision. Here, §2255(h) directs that a second-or-successive federal-prisoner motion may proceed only if it is “certified as provided in section 2244,” and that cross-reference most naturally carries with it §2244(b)(1)’s first-step bar on relitigating claims previously presented—so Bowe’s repeat claim fails at that antecedent statutory hurdle without reaching any further equitable or merits inquiry. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E) uses unequivocal “shall not … be the subject of … a writ of certiorari” language barring certiorari review of the court of appeals’ authorization decision, and nothing in this record suggests an alternative jurisdictional vehicle properly before us that would allow merits review notwithstanding that statutory limit. Even if one thought the result harsh in light of later legal developments, AEDPA’s structure (including strict timing and successive-filing limits) reflects Congress’s chosen balance, and our duty is to enforce those conditions rather than revise them.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The dispositive question is textual: § 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies only to an “application under section 2254,” so it does not cover federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions under § 2255, and the Eleventh Circuit’s contrary rule (treating § 2244(b)(1) as incorporated via § 2255(h)’s cross-reference) extends the statute beyond its enacted text. The circuit landscape reflects a developed split on that precise question, underscoring the need for a uniform national rule and reinforcing that the better reading is the one anchored in the limiting words Congress chose. On jurisdiction, § 2244(b)(3)(E) bars certiorari review of the court of appeals’ grant/denial of authorization decisions, but it does not strip this Court of power to resolve the statutory question through an appropriate vehicle that is not a direct challenge to an authorization order, and the existence of entrenched disagreement counsels against reading (E) to make the conflict effectively unreviewable. Applying those principles to Bowe’s Davis-based successive request, the relitigation bar in § 2244(b)(1) should not categorically foreclose his § 2255 motion solely because he previously presented the same claim in a prior successive application.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA’s successive-petition scheme is a deliberate funneling mechanism, and §2255(h)’s express cross-reference to §2244’s gatekeeping framework is best read to import not only the authorization procedure but also the core anti-relitigation rule of §2244(b)(1), preventing federal prisoners from re-presenting claims in a second-or-successive motion after a first §2255. That reading fits AEDPA’s structural emphasis on finality and Congress’s willingness to tolerate harsh timing and retroactivity consequences for later-decided Supreme Court cases (as reflected in Dodd and §2255(f)(3)), rather than permitting end-runs around the successive-motion limits. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s text (“shall not be ... the subject of ... a writ of certiorari”) forecloses this Court’s ordinary certiorari review of the court of appeals’ gatekeeping/authorization determination, and under jurisdictional first principles we should not reach merits questions in a posture Congress has barred. Felker indicates Congress may restrict certiorari over these gatekeeping determinations while leaving other avenues (e.g., original habeas) theoretically available, so the certiorari bar applies as written here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying the statute as written, §2244(b)(1) regulates only a “claim presented in a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and a federal prisoner’s §2255 motion is not an “application under section 2254”; §2255(h)’s limited cross-reference to “the procedure for certification” in §2244 does not clearly incorporate §2244(b)(1)’s separate relitigation bar. Consistent with Banister and Magwood, “second or successive” is a term of art anchored in giving a prisoner one fair opportunity for merits review while reserving AEDPA’s strict hurdles for filings that truly fall within the specified gatekeeping regime—here, Congress expressly chose different textual triggers for state (§2254) and federal (§2255) collateral review. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) blocks certiorari from the court of appeals’ gatekeeping authorization decision, but it should not be read to insulate from this Court’s review the antecedent, purely legal question whether §2244(b)(1) applies to §2255 at all; otherwise an acknowledged split on a recurring federal question becomes effectively unreviewable. Pre-AEDPA practice and miscarriage-of-justice principles further counsel against extending §2244(b)(1) beyond its textual scope where doing so would categorically foreclose certain legally innocent prisoners from ever obtaining federal merits consideration of new, retroactive Supreme Court decisions.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s bar on repeating previously presented claims in second-or-successive habeas litigation—28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1)—applies to federal prisoners filing second-or-successive motions to vacate under 28 U.S.C. §2255, and whether §2244(b)(3)(E) prevents Supreme Court certiorari review of courts of appeals’ authorization decisions in that context.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 2244(b)(1), 2244(b)(3)(E), and 2255 (including §2255(h) governing second-or-successive motions, and (as discussed in the materials) §2255(f)(3) governing limitations periods tied to newly recognized rights).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1) by its text governs only state-prisoner habeas petitions under §2254 (it speaks in terms of a prior “application” for habeas corpus), and Congress did not incorporate §2244(b)(1) into §2255’s second-or-successive regime for federal prisoners (instead using §2255(h) as the exclusive gatekeeping standard). He further argues that reading §2244(b)(1) to apply to §2255 creates arbitrary and unjust results—blocking federal prisoners from obtaining merits review even when the Supreme Court later announces and makes retroactive a new constitutional rule—and that the Court should clarify it has jurisdiction to review authorization decisions notwithstanding §2244(b)(3)(E), because otherwise the circuit split becomes effectively unreviewable and entrenched.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that Congress designed AEDPA to promote finality and to sharply limit repetitive postconviction litigation, and that it is neither ‘unfair’ nor ‘unusual’ for diligent federal prisoners to be unable to benefit from later changes in law. It contends §2244(b)(1)’s claim-repetition bar appropriately applies to §2255 second-or-successive litigation, preventing relitigation of the same claim across multiple rounds (often after the prisoner has already had several opportunities to raise it, including direct appeal, an initial §2255 motion, and an authorization request). On jurisdiction, the government position reflected in the materials is that §2244(b)(3)(E) is at least a substantial obstacle to certiorari review of authorization grants/denials, and thus the Court should be cautious about reaching beyond what AEDPA permits.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (statement respecting denial of certiorari by Justice Kavanaugh)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (statement respecting denial by Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Jackson)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is the textual one: §2244(b)(1) expressly speaks of an “application under section 2254,” and we should hesitate to extend a scoped substantive bar by implication. But §2255(h) does more than borrow a generic procedure; it requires certification “as provided in section 2244,” and, as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, §2244(b)(3)(C) instructs the court of appeals to decide whether the filing “satisfies the requirements of this subsection”—language that naturally calls for applying the subsection’s operative limits, including the relitigation command in (b)(1), rather than treating it as optional surplus. Reading the cross-reference to exclude (b)(1) would create the very structural gap Justice Alito identifies, permitting repetitive re-presentations at the authorization stage and undermining AEDPA’s channeling and finality objectives. On reviewability, I remain persuaded that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical no-certiorari rule attaches to decisions made within the incorporated §2244(b)(3) mechanism, and we should not evade that jurisdictional limit by relabeling the determination.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is that §2255(h)’s command of certification “as provided in section 2244,” combined with §2244(b)(3)(C)’s reference to “requirements of this subsection,” naturally pulls in §2244(b)(1). But that reading ignores the statute’s own scope limitation: §2244(b)(1) applies only to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and a cross-reference to an authorization mechanism cannot silently expand a substantively cabined rule to a different remedial vehicle when Congress separately and exclusively specified §2255(h)’s gateways. Justice Alito’s “structural gap” concern is ultimately remedied by the scheme Congress enacted—§2255(h)’s strict gateways and the term-of-art limits on what counts as second-or-successive—not by judicially importing §2254-specific dismissals. For the same reason, I cannot read §2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar to strip our jurisdiction over §2255(h) authorizations absent clear text extending that jurisdictional limitation beyond §2244(b)’s §2254-centered regime.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the best textual objection: §2244(b)(1) expressly speaks of “application[s] under section 2254,” and §2255(h) does not repeat that phrase. But §2255(h) does more than borrow a generic procedure; it requires certification “as provided in section 2244,” and, as Justice Barrett and the Chief observe, §2244(b)(3)(C) then instructs the court of appeals to decide whether the filing satisfies “the requirements of this subsection”—language that naturally incorporates subsection (b)(1)’s mandatory relitigation bar rather than treating it as an inapplicable ornament. The petitioners’ reading slices the cross-reference into disconnected parts and creates a structural gap that would allow federal prisoners to re-present identical claims indefinitely at the authorization stage, a result difficult to reconcile with AEDPA’s integrated, rule-like constraints designed to promote finality and conserve judicial resources. On reviewability, I remain aligned with the Chief and Justice Gorsuch that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical no-certiorari command attaches to determinations made within the §2244(b)(3) mechanism that §2255(h) expressly invokes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s integrated-scheme argument is the strongest point for Respondent: §2255(h)’s cross-reference to certification “as provided in section 2244,” coupled with §2244(b)(3)(C)’s instruction to test “the requirements of this subsection,” plausibly reads as importing (b)(1). But that reading still treats the cross-reference as silently expanding a substantive relitigation bar that Congress expressly confined to “application[s] under section 2254,” and I agree with Justices Kagan and Kavanaugh that the scope limitation in §2244(b)(1) cannot be written out as mere surplusage. Consistent with Magwood’s instruction that “second or successive” is a term of art informed by pre-AEDPA practice, §2255(h)’s two gateways should remain the exclusive substantive limits for federal prisoners, with §2244(b)(3) supplying the screening mechanism rather than additional categorical bars. For similar reasons, I am not persuaded by Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reading of §2244(b)(3)(E) to strip this Court’s certiorari jurisdiction in §2255 cases absent a clearer statement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Barrett make the best point for Respondent: §2255(h)’s instruction that a motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” coupled with §2244(b)(3)(C)’s reference to “requirements of this subsection,” suggests an integrated gatekeeping scheme that would include §2244(b)(1). But that reading still cannot get around the hard textual boundary that §2244(b)(1) applies only to an “application under section 2254”; importing it would expand a substantive relitigation bar Congress expressly limited, even though Congress elsewhere in AEDPA wrote §2255-specific successive-motion rules. Consistent with Slack/Panetti’s treatment of “second or successive” as a term of art informed by abuse-of-the-writ practice, the better construction is that §2255(h) supplies the exclusive substantive gateways while §2244(b)(3) supplies the certification procedure—avoiding an atextual superaddition. And Justice Alito’s finality concern, while real, cannot justify extending §2244(b)(3)(E)’s jurisdiction-stripping beyond its clear statutory home to insulate a threshold legal error about what standard governs §2255(h) authorizations.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Kagan press the hardest point: §2244(b)(1) expressly addresses only a successive “application under section 2254,” and we should be wary of enlarging that scope by implication. But §2255(h) does not incorporate some free-floating “procedure”; it commands certification “as provided in section 2244,” and, as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, §2244(b)(3)(C) imposes a mandatory rule of decision—authorization turns on whether the filing “satisfies the requirements of this subsection,” which includes (b)(1)’s relitigation bar. Reading the cross-reference to import only mechanics while excluding the subsection’s interlocking “shall dismiss/shall not” limits would create the structural gap Justice Alito identifies and is difficult to reconcile with AEDPA’s cumulative gatekeeping design. For the same reason, I continue to read §2244(b)(3)(E)’s no-certiorari command as categorical for decisions made within the §2244(b)(3) mechanism that §2255(h) invokes; we are not at liberty to carve out reviewability exceptions where Congress has spoken in jurisdictional terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is the integrated-scheme reading: because §2255(h) requires certification “as provided in section 2244,” they say §2244(b)(3)(C)’s reference to “the requirements of this subsection” necessarily pulls in §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar. But §2244(b)(1) contains an express scope limitation—“application under section 2254”—and I do not think we should treat a cross-reference to an authorization mechanism as silently overriding that limitation and expanding a substantive bar Congress drafted to apply only to a different class of cases. The more natural textual reading is that §2255(h) incorporates §2244(b)(3)’s procedure (who decides, timing, prima facie standard), while §2255(h) itself supplies the exclusive substantive gateways for federal prisoners, consistent with Justice Thomas’s point about separate calibration. On reviewability, I remain unpersuaded by Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s categorical reading of §2244(b)(3)(E); extending a jurisdiction-stripping provision beyond its §2254-centered text requires clearer congressional direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest point from Justices Kavanaugh and Kagan is the scope clause in §2244(b)(1)—its reference to “application[s] under section 2254” is real textual resistance to incorporation. But §2255(h) does not simply borrow a generic procedure; as the Chief Justice explains, it requires certification “as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) then directs the court of appeals to decide whether the filing “satisfies the requirements of this subsection,” which most naturally includes the subsection’s mandatory relitigation bar rather than treating it as an optional add-on. Justice Thomas’s view that the cross-reference imports only mechanics underreads the integrated “shall dismiss/shall not … unless” design and would create the structural gap Justice Alito identifies, permitting endless re-presentation of identical claims at the authorization stage. For similar reasons, I agree with Justices Roberts and Gorsuch that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s no-certiorari command attaches to authorization determinations made within the very §2244(b)(3) mechanism that §2255(h) expressly invokes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I have engaged carefully with the Chief Justice’s and Justice Barrett’s integrated-structure point that §2255(h)’s “certified as provided in section 2244,” combined with §2244(b)(3)(C)’s reference to “requirements of this subsection,” necessarily carries in §2244(b)(1). But that argument still cannot overcome the limiting text Congress chose in §2244(b)(1): it is expressly confined to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and treating “as provided” as silently expanding that scope reads past a clear statutory boundary. Justice Alito’s and Justice Gorsuch’s “structural gap” concern is a policy objection that AEDPA already addresses through §2255(h)’s two exclusive gateways and through the term-of-art limits on what constitutes a new “application” or “claim” under Gonzalez/Banister/Magwood, without adding a categorical, nontextual relitigation bar. For the same reasons, I do not see §2244(b)(3)(E)’s no-certiorari command as an unmistakably clear jurisdictional bar for §2255(h) authorization errors simply because §2255(h) borrows the §2244(b)(3) mechanism.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA was enacted to curb repetitive collateral attacks and to promote finality, and §2255(h) expressly incorporates §2244’s gatekeeping mechanism; reading §2244(b)(1)’s claim-repetition bar as applicable in the §2255 successive-motion context best fits that integrated scheme and prevents end-runs around Congress’s deliberately demanding thresholds. The question is not whether it would be equitable to allow relitigation after later legal developments, but whether Congress authorized it; absent clear statutory permission, federal courts should not expand successive-review beyond AEDPA’s text and purpose. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E) by its terms bars certiorari review of a court of appeals’ authorization decision, and Felker indicates that such a limitation is constitutionally permissible so long as other avenues (e.g., original habeas) are not foreclosed; this case does not present the exceptional circumstance requiring us to override that statutory bar. Accordingly, I would uphold application of §2244(b)(1) to successive §2255 proceedings and treat §2244(b)(3)(E) as precluding certiorari review of the authorization ruling here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: AEDPA’s postconviction scheme channels federal prisoners’ successive litigation through §2255(h), which enumerates the exclusive two gateways for a second-or-successive motion, and it does not incorporate §2244(b)(1)’s separate, state-habeas claim-repetition bar. Section 2244(b)(1) speaks in terms of an “application” under §2254’s regime, and when Congress meant AEDPA provisions to apply to §2255 it said so expressly elsewhere—so extending §2244(b)(1) to §2255 would be judicial rewriting rather than text-and-structure interpretation. As to review, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari” targets authorization decisions under §2244(b)(3), i.e., the §2254 gatekeeping mechanism; it does not unambiguously strip this Court’s certiorari jurisdiction over courts of appeals’ §2255(h) authorizations, and any such withdrawal of jurisdiction must be found in the statute Congress actually enacted. On these facts, Bowe’s successive request must rise or fall under §2255(h) alone, without an extra-textual §2244(b)(1) categorical bar or an unwarranted jurisdictional extension of §2244(b)(3)(E).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA establishes an integrated, habeas-specific procedural regime designed to prevent repetitive litigation and to promote finality, and §2244(b)(1)’s categorical command that a previously presented claim “shall be dismissed” fits that design and should not be softened by importing ordinary civil-procedure instincts. Reading §2255(h) as the exclusive successive-motion rule would create a structural gap—allowing federal prisoners to re-present identical claims in successive rounds so long as they can clear (or attempt to clear) authorization—undermining the interlocking constraints Congress enacted. The fact that §2244(b)’s language is framed in terms of “applications” and §2254 does not defeat its function in the overall architecture that Congress applied to postconviction, judgment-based custody challenges, and any asserted harshness is the sort of consequence AEDPA deliberately accepts in service of efficiency and finality. Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s no-review provision at least strongly counsels against certiorari review of courts of appeals’ authorization determinations in this context, because allowing plenary Supreme Court review would dilute AEDPA’s gatekeeping design and reintroduce delay at the very stage Congress sought to make swift and final.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Magwood, “second or successive” is a term of art, so we do not reflexively import §2244(b)(1)’s state-prisoner claim-repetition rule into the distinct §2255(h) gatekeeping scheme absent a clear congressional directive. Looking to the pre-AEDPA baseline, repetitive federal collateral attacks were constrained but not categorically barred in the rigid manner the Government urges, and AEDPA’s text chose to regulate federal prisoners’ successive filings through §2255(h)’s two narrow gateways rather than by cross-applying §2244(b)(1) wholesale. A purposive check confirms the point: applying §2244(b)(1) to §2255 would arbitrarily foreclose merits consideration even where a later, retroactive Supreme Court decision supplies the very kind of new rule AEDPA elsewhere contemplates, a departure from historical practice not clearly commanded by the statute. On reviewability, consistent with narrow construction of jurisdiction-stripping provisions, §2244(b)(3)(E) should not be read to insulate from certiorari a court of appeals’ threshold, legally inapplicable “jurisdictional” disposition of an authorization request in the §2255 context.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms regulates “second or successive habeas corpus application[s] under section 2254,” and Congress in §2255(h) created a distinct, self-contained gatekeeping regime for federal prisoners—requiring only that a successive motion be “certified as provided,” not importing §2244(b)(1)’s separate claim-repetition bar. Reading “second or successive” as a term of art (Slack; Panetti) anchored in pre-AEDPA abuse-of-the-writ practice confirms that AEDPA’s restrictions attach where a prisoner is truly launching a new, abusive round of litigation, not whenever a later filing repeats a claim that could become newly viable because of intervening retroactive law—especially given §2255’s remedial-equivalence to habeas and its saving-clause backstop. And §2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar, again textually tied to the §2254 authorization scheme, should not be extended to insulate from this Court’s review a threshold legal error about what standards govern §2255(h) authorizations absent a clear congressional statement. Because the court of appeals denied authorization by applying an inapplicable statutory bar, I would reverse and allow the §2255(h) authorization decision to be made under the correct standard with this Court retaining jurisdiction to correct that category mistake.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Congress supplied a mandatory rule of decision in AEDPA: a prisoner “shall” not proceed with second-or-successive collateral litigation unless the statutory gatekeeping conditions are satisfied, and courts must apply each applicable barrier cumulatively rather than stopping after one favorable test. Here, §2255(h) expressly imports §2244’s authorization mechanism, and in that structure §2244(b)(1)’s relitigation bar functions as an independent threshold against repeating the same “claim,” with §2255(h) then supplying additional, narrower conditions for any genuinely new claim to go forward. Separately, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s command that authorization decisions “shall not be the subject of … certiorari” must be respected as written; as in prior cases, the Court may not evade Congress’s jurisdictional limits by recharacterizing the inquiry. Even if the petitioner asserts unfairness, AEDPA’s finality-centered limits are for Congress to relax, and equitable habeas discretion cannot be used to override an applicable “shall not … unless” statutory bar.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Starting with the statutory text, § 2244(b)(1) by its terms regulates only a "second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254," and under ordinary negative-implication reasoning Congress’s express reference to § 2254—and omission of § 2255—means the claim-repetition bar does not apply to federal prisoners’ successive § 2255 motions, which instead are governed by § 2255(h)’s distinct gatekeeping criteria. The courts of appeals are entrenchedly divided on that question, and the United States’ litigating position (agreeing that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255) is a significant institutional cue that the contrary multi-circuit rule is inconsistent with the text, making the issue certworthy and warranting correction. On the jurisdictional point, § 2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari limitation is likewise embedded in the § 2244(b) authorization framework that applies to § 2254 "applications," so reading it to bar this Court’s review of § 2255 authorization decisions extends the provision beyond its textual scope and would unnecessarily insulate the split from resolution. Accordingly, I would reverse the judgment applying § 2244(b)(1) to § 2255 and reject the asserted certiorari bar in this § 2255 context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: AEDPA’s postconviction scheme deliberately channels second-or-successive federal collateral attacks through a tightly constrained gatekeeping process, and §2255(h)’s command that a successive motion be certified “as provided in section 2244” incorporates §2244(b)’s screening requirements as integral features of that design rather than technicalities to be evaded. Reading §2244(b)(3)(C) to require a prima facie showing that the application “satisfies the requirements of this subsection” naturally brings along the subsection’s core anti-repetition rule—§2244(b)(1)’s dismissal of claims already presented—so a federal prisoner may not relitigate the same claim in a successive §2255 motion even if later authority strengthens the argument. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s bar on certiorari from authorization decisions reflects Congress’s choice to make the courts of appeals’ gatekeeping determinations largely final, and concerns about unfairness from later changes in law cannot override those structural and textual limits. This follows the same channeling-and-finality logic we apply elsewhere: unavailability of further collateral review is a feature of the statutory design, not a reason to create an alternative path.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Starting with AEDPA’s statutory architecture, a federal prisoner ordinarily gets “one fair opportunity” for merits review via an initial §2255 motion, and Congress then imposed a sharply limited second-or-successive gateway in §2255(h) plus the authorization procedure in §2244(b)(3)—but §2255(h) does not textually incorporate §2244(b)(1)’s separate claim-repetition bar. Treating “second or successive” as a term of art (Banister; Magwood) reinforces that we must classify the later filing by what Congress actually regulated: for federal prisoners, the operative merits screen for successive motions is §2255(h)’s narrow categories, not an extra, non-incorporated §2244(b)(1) dismissal rule. And under Gonzalez’s distinction between an “application” seeking merits adjudication of a federal “claim” and other filings, a successive §2255 motion is indeed a merits-seeking application—but the question is which successive limits apply, and the best reading is that §2255(h) supplies them without importing §2244(b)(1). Finally, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar should be read, consistent with this Court’s usual reluctance to infer jurisdiction-stripping beyond clear text, to apply to “this section” (state-prisoner §2244) authorization decisions and not to foreclose this Court’s review of courts of appeals’ §2255(h) authorization rulings where Congress did not clearly say so.
